introduction: From 1911 to 1913 ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, nearly seventy and newly free after forty years as a prisoner and exile, travelled to Egypt, Europe and North America. The guide follows the journey in his own letters and remarks: notes written walking in a park or on a steamship, invitations, the frank business of costs and health, the refusal of gifts, exhaustion, homecoming, and afterwards the question whether the seed has grown. The nearest companion is Paul: his travel plans and apologies, his “journeyings often”, his night vision of a man asking for help across the sea, his day before the philosophers of Athens, his “these hands have ministered unto my necessities”. Around them stand a few voices from the age itself, Kipling’s East and West, Tennyson’s railways, the lines on the Statue of Liberty he saluted. Thomas à Kempis, Pascal and Emerson distrust travel on principle, and their distrust clarifies what kind of journey this was.
questions: Paul wrote, “I will come to you … if the Lord permit”, and apologized for delays. What do the practical letters in this guide (winter, expenses, health) add to our picture of a spiritual mission?
He refused all contributions; Paul says “these hands have ministered unto my necessities”. Why did both think this mattered?
Kempis says wanderers seldom become holy, and Pascal that misery comes from not staying in one’s room. What distinguishes this journey from the restlessness they warn of?
“Its importance is not now manifest” (198). How should the results of such a journey be judged, and when?
Emerson calls travelling a fool’s paradise. What do readings 199 to 202 ask of those who were visited, as distinct from the one who travelled?

outside.why: He writes while walking in a park, “as I have absolutely no free time”. Mark of Jesus and the twelve: there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.

A letter written on a steamship amid the waves. The elder to a friend: I had many things to write, but I will not with ink and pen write unto thee: I trust I shall shortly see thee, and we shall speak face to face.
His fatigue left him when he saw the believers’ faces. Paul: God is my record, how greatly I long after you all.
A prisoner of forty years comes to San Francisco. When the Lord turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that dream.
Paul reckoned his imprisonment the same way: the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel.
“It is dawn and I am walking.” Rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place.

He salutes the Statue of Liberty from the deck with open arms. The lines on its pedestal: give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free; I lift my lamp beside the golden door.
Broadway’s electric signs amuse him. Thoreau on such things: our inventions are wont to be pretty toys, improved means to an unimproved end.
“Where is Acca—where is Los Angeles?” Yet hearts are near. Though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit.

Thousands of miles crossed, to show how much he longed to meet them. Paul planned as far: having a great desire these many years to come unto you, whensoever I take my journey into Spain, I will come to you.
Thomas à Kempis held that they who wander much abroad seldom thereby become holy. The cloister’s wisdom is against journeys. What made this one different in kind from wandering?
“We have traversed the expanse” of the ocean. They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters; these see the works of the Lord.
A great stirring arose and grand gatherings formed. Said of Paul’s company in one city: these that have turned the world upside down are come hither also.
Peace societies and reformers invite him to America. A vision appeared to Paul in the night: there stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us.
Invitations from conferences, governors and the eminent. The queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon and came to prove him with hard questions; here the East is asked to come West.
The friends rejoice at news of his coming. How shall they hear without a preacher? and how shall they preach, except they be sent?

“Responsibilities are surging like ocean waves.” Martha was cumbered about much serving. Even a holy errand has its burden of arrangements; what do these practical letters show about how he carried it?
“My presence there in winter time is somewhat difficult.” Paul to Timothy: do thy diligence to come before winter.
Preparing in Egypt for the journey. Paul’s travel plans read the same: I will tarry at Ephesus until Pentecost, for a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries.

“I am about to depart for the West.” Paul setting out for Jerusalem: I go bound in the spirit, not knowing the things that shall befall me; neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy.
Unwell in Egypt, and warned that the sea is wide. Tennyson’s Ulysses, old: old age hath yet his honour and his toil; some work of noble note may yet be done.
Ill before leaving, he felt better once embarked on service. They that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall run, and not be weary.
A bishop says no one has come from East to West with such an aim. Many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down in the kingdom.
Kipling’s ballad, published twenty years earlier, begins “East is East, and West is West” and ends: there is neither East nor West, when two strong men stand face to face.
The verses of divine unity proclaimed in every gathering. Paul on the Areopagus, to a learned and curious city: God hath made of one blood all nations of men.
He spoke to the eminent in great assemblies. At Athens some mocked, and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter; howbeit certain men clave unto him.
From place to place through nine states. Ye shall be witnesses unto me unto the uttermost part of the earth.

Two years away, leaving all his concerns. In journeyings often, in weariness and painfulness, in watchings often; beside those things that are without, that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the churches.
“O how we miss you!” We, brethren, being taken from you for a short time in presence, not in heart, endeavoured the more abundantly to see your face.
The call was raised in great churches and assemblies. This thing was not done in a corner.
One day London, another Edinburgh, Paris, Stuttgart, Budapest, Vienna. Tennyson on the new age of rail: let the great world spin for ever down the ringing grooves of change.
He passed through the world’s famous resorts and would not stop for them. Shown all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, Jesus declined. What is a traveller who is not a tourist?
“Each day in a different city, each hour in a different place.” They confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
“Like a bird without nest or shelter.” The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.

Three years wandering like the desert wind. Pascal: all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber. He meant restlessness. How is the restlessness of these letters different?
No rest day or night in Europe. I will very gladly spend and be spent for you.
For four years he called in every gathering; capacity varied. In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand: for thou knowest not whether shall prosper.
“America cannot be compared to Europe. It is another world.” Tocqueville had found the difference in its people’s habit of forming associations for every purpose.
The friends must now adopt his manner and conduct. I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you.
He had never given a speech before, and plunged in. Moses: I am not eloquent; and the answer: I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say.
So tired that his voice would not carry. My strength is made perfect in weakness.
Without power to utter a word, he turned before entering the meeting. O Lord, open thou my lips; and my mouth shall shew forth thy praise.
He would accept no contributions for the journey. Paul’s farewell to Ephesus: I have coveted no man’s silver, or gold, or apparel; these hands have ministered unto my necessities.
Gifts were refused, and given away. Freely ye have received, freely give.
The expenses of a travelling party are reckoned frankly. Which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost?
No chance to answer letters since arriving in the West. Paul apologizes to a church in the same strain: we would have come unto you, once and again; but Satan hindered us.
The journey told terribly on his constitution. Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.
Three meetings a day and interviews till midnight. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course.
Arrived at Port Said, he forgot every hardship. The Lord shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth.
The journey has brought forth results. Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest.
“Its importance is not now manifest.” I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.

Will he come again? If results appear. Emerson told Americans that travelling is a fool’s paradise: our first journeys discover to us the indifference of places. He was speaking to those who go abroad to find what they lack. What does his rule say to those who wait for a visitor to bring it?
“If America becomes illumined, its illumination, like a magnet, will draw me there.” Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in.
Pray for harmony, that your country may be fit for his presence. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!

shortfall: Many readings are travel notes (dates, sailings, arrangements, health) that have no companion beyond those given to their kind; they were left as they are.
